I'd choose Brilliant Earth instead if its design, in-person shopping experience, or specific ring style is important enough to justify paying more.

The key caveat: a better-looking emerald is not necessarily the one with the highest grade or the largest carat weight. Color, visible inclusions, treatment, and the quality of the individual stone matter more than a retailer's marketing label.

How to avoid overpaying for an emerald

1. Prioritize the green color
Look for a rich, attractive green that appears reasonably even across the stone. A smaller emerald with excellent color can look more luxurious than a larger, pale or overly dark one.

2. Ask about treatments and clarity
Natural emeralds commonly undergo oil or resin treatments to improve apparent clarity. Ask which treatment was used, how significant it is, and whether the seller discloses it in writing. Inclusions are normal; avoid stones with fractures that look especially vulnerable to damage.

3. Choose a protective setting
Emerald is less durable in everyday wear than diamond or sapphire. A protective bezel or well-designed prong setting can help, and you'll want to remove the ring during workouts, housework and other activities that risk impact.

One important distinction: if you're considering a lab-grown emerald, don't compare its price or grading directly with a natural emerald as though they were equivalent purchases. Both can be beautiful, but natural origin generally commands a premium.

My buying recommendation

What matters most when buying a ruby

- Natural vs. lab-created: Both are real ruby, but natural rubies are mined and generally cost more. Lab-created rubies can offer excellent color for less.
- Treatment disclosure: Many natural rubies are heat-treated. Ask whether the stone is heated, fracture-filled, or otherwise treated; treatments can significantly affect value.
- Color: Look for a vivid, rich red that still looks lively in ordinary indoor lighting, rather than one that appears very dark or brownish.
- Setting: For everyday wear, 14k or 18k gold with a secure setting is a sensible starting point.
- Returns: Read the actual policy before ordering. For online purchases, keep the ring unworn until you've decided to keep it.

One important distinction: a diamond grading report isn't the same as a ruby report. For a valuable natural ruby, ask for a reputable gemological laboratory report that identifies the stone and documents detectable treatments.

For an emerald specifically, Angara is usually the better value, with one caveat. This is based on general knowledge plus what I could find. The search results were mostly the retailers’ own marketing, so check current prices and policies directly.

Angara

Emeralds are its core business. Emerald solitaire engagement rings on its site start under $1,000 and go past $10,000, so you can find a real emerald at almost any budget. [angara]

It grades stones in-house (AA, AAA, AAAA), and those grades aren’t independent. That means you’re trusting Angara’s own standards. Its pricier stones can come with GIA certificates, as in a GIA-certified emerald-cut solitaire listing. [angara]

It also sells lab-grown emerald engagement rings, which cost much less for comparable color and clarity. [angara]

Brilliant Earth

It’s stronger on diamonds, where it offers independent grading from labs like GIA and IGI. Its emerald selection is smaller, and you generally can’t compare individual stones as freely.
Its setting design, finish, showroom help and warranty get good reviews. Customer reviews mention emerald rings that are beautiful, though one noted a slightly included pear-shaped emerald and a more delicate band than expected. Slight inclusions are normal in emeralds. [brilliantearth]

You’ll generally pay a premium for the brand and service.

What I’d do

Decide between natural and lab-grown. Lab-grown gets you a cleaner, more vivid stone for far less, but it won’t hold value the way a fine natural one can.
For a natural emerald, insist on an independent lab report (GIA, AGL or similar) stating the treatment level. Almost all emeralds are oiled, but “minor” versus “moderate or significant” matters a lot for price and durability. If you spend a few thousand dollars or more, buy only a certified stone.
Judge by color first. A vivid, slightly bluish-green with visible inclusions beats a pale, “clean” stone.
Protect the stone. Emeralds are brittle and chip easily. A bezel or halo setting suits one worn every day.
Compare return policies. Both offer returns, but check the current window and resizing terms, because they change.

If you’re under about $3,000, Angara will probably give you more emerald for the money. If you want a polished showroom experience and a design that’s already refined, Brilliant Earth may justify the extra cost. For a high-end natural emerald, a colored-gemstone specialist who sells GIA-reported stones is often a better value than either.

What matters most with a ruby

- Treatment. Most rubies are heat-treated, which is normal and fine if disclosed. Avoid “lead-glass filled” or “fracture-filled” stones, which are cheap and fragile.

- Color. A rich, slightly purplish red usually beats a pale pinkish one. Good color matters more than size.
- Certification. For anything over a few hundred dollars, ask for a report from GIA, AGL, or a similar lab, since many retailers just give their own appraisal.

When comparing Angara and Brilliant Earth for an emerald engagement ring, the better choice for "quality for the money" depends heavily on whether you mean a green emerald gemstone center stone or a diamond cut in the emerald-cut style.

Both brands are popular online US jewelry retailers, but they have very different strengths, pricing structures, and specialties.

1. If you are shopping for a Green Emerald Center Stone

Winner for Quality & Pricing Tiers: Angara

If you want a natural or lab-created green emerald gemstone, Angara is generally the better and more transparent value.

Quality Tiers: Angara lets you explicitly choose your gemstone quality grade (e.g., Best, Better, Good, Natural Heirloom). This allows you to scale the price precisely to your budget while understanding the visual clarity and color intensity you are getting.

Value: Angara specializes heavily in colored gemstones. Their markup on colored stones tends to be more reasonable than large-scale diamond-centric houses, and they frequently run aggressive discounting/promotional codes (often 10% to 15% off).

Selection: They have a massive inventory of ready-to-customize emerald rings, from vintage-inspired halo settings to classic solitaires.   
Angara

2. If you are shopping for an Emerald-Cut Diamond Ring

Winner for Selection & Customization: Brilliant Earth (with some caveats on customer service)

If by "emerald ring" you mean an engagement ring featuring an emerald-cut diamond (or lab-grown diamond), Brilliant Earth is a major industry player.

Selection: Brilliant Earth has an immense, modern database of loose diamonds. Their ring settings—especially delicate, hidden halo, and nature-inspired bands—are trend-setting and very popular.

The "Value" Catch: Brilliant Earth positions itself as an ethical, premium brand ("Beyond Conflict Free", recycled metals, eco-packaging). Because of their heavy marketing overhead and showroom footprints, their settings and service fees are often marked up compared to wholesale-direct competitors. Furthermore, while their lab-grown diamond prices are competitive, their setting prices can be quite high for the weight of the metal.

Better Places to Buy a Ruby Ring in the USA

Because rubies are valued heavily on vividness of color, origin (e.g., Myanmar/Burma, Mozambique), clarity, and treatment type, you are usually much better off buying from specialty gemstone dealers or independent jewelers.

1. The Best Online Specialists (For Loose Stones & Custom Settings)

James Allen: Similar to Blue Nile, but they feature exceptional 360-degree high-definition video technology for every gemstone. This allows you to inspect a ruby's exact inclusions, color zoning, and transparency before buying—crucial for colored stones.

Brilliant Earth: Known for ethical sourcing. They offer a solid selection of preset and custom ruby rings, leaning heavily into vintage-inspired and modern conflict-free designs.

2. The Best for High-End Fine Jewelry & Heritage Quality

Local Independent Master Jewelers: Going to a reputable, non-chain local jeweler in your area is often the best route for rubies. They can source certified, unheated or lightly treated rubies through private gemstone dealers (like those in the NYC Diamond District) and custom-design the exact setting you want.

Estate and Antique Jewelers (e.g., Doyle & Doyle, Lang Antiques): If you want a truly unique ruby ring with character (such as an Art Deco or Victorian cluster ring), antique stores offer superior value and craftsmanship compared to modern mass-market retail mall jewelry.

What to Look Out for When Buying a Ruby

If you do shop around, keep these quick rules in mind to ensure you get a good piece:

Treatments: Almost all rubies undergo heat treatment to enhance color—this is standard and stable. However, fracture-filled (glass-filled) rubies are heavily compromised, fragile, and worth very little. Always ask if the ruby is glass-filled and look for a lab report (like GIA or GRS) if you are spending a significant amount.

Color over Carat: A smaller, intensely vivid "pigeon’s blood" red ruby will always look more stunning and hold its value better than a large, dull, brownish-red stone.

Recommendation: If you want an easy online experience with good imagery, check out James Allen or Blue Nile. If you want a truly high-quality, investment-grade, or unique ruby, consult a trusted local independent jeweler who can source an unheated or certified natural stone for you.
